dialogue.shona: Zvirevo nemadimikira zvaishandiswa kupanana mazano akadzama.
dialogue.english: Proverbs and idioms were used to share deep advice with one another.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Zvirevo [things revo] • nemadimikira [and / with madimikira] • zvaishandiswa [zvaishandiswa] • kupanana [to / at panana] • mazano [plural zano] • akadzama [he/she (past) dzama]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akadzama')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akadzama' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nemadimikira'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nemadimikira'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'madimikira' forms 'nemadimikira'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('zvaishandiswa')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'zvaishandiswa' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

cultural_notes.title: The Treasury of Shona Proverbs ('Zvirevo') & Idioms ('Madimikira')
cultural_notes.content: Shona is famous for its thousands of proverbs ('zvirevo' / 'tsumo') and figurative idioms ('madimikira'). Elders calls proverbs 'the salt of speech'—using them to offer gentle counsel ('mazano akadzama') without harshness.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you politely ask someone to speak softly ('taura zvinyoronyoro')?
In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).
